source.title: Distal Biceps Tendon Injuries in Athletes: Management Strategies, Return-to-Sport Predictors, and Performance Outcomes

paper.citation: Phrathep D., Colon D., Schoch B.S., Pagan-Rosado R.D. Distal Biceps Tendon Injuries in Athletes: Management Strategies, Return-to-Sport Predictors, and Performance Outcomes. Current Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation Reports. 2026;14(1):21. doi:10.1007/s40141-026-00546-5.
paper.abstract: This paper addresses the following question: What does the current literature indicate about diagnosis, management, rehabilitation, return-to-sport predictors, and performance outcomes after distal biceps tendon injury in athletes? Participants: No new cohort; evidence summarized from injured patients and athletes. Sport and level: General active populations, strength athletes, and professional American-football players. Design: Current narrative review. Exposure or intervention: Operative and nonoperative management, surgical approaches, and rehabilitation strategies.
paper.tldr: In a cited meta-analysis of 2,481 cases, operative treatment was associated with higher flexion strength and endurance, higher supination strength and endurance, and better MEPS and DASH scores than nonoperative treatment; these are pooled clinical associations, not randomized causal estimates. Across the reviewed athletic literature, reported return-to-sport rates after repair ranged from 91.5% to 97.5%; 65.6% returned at the same or higher intensity, while another synthesis reported 93.4% returning at any level. For a high-demand athlete with a suspected complete rupture, the review supports prompt specialist assessment and a shared medical decision that weighs sport demands, injury features, and athlete preferences.
paper.methods: Design: Current narrative review. Exposure or intervention: Operative and nonoperative management, surgical approaches, and rehabilitation strategies. Comparator: Treatment and technique comparisons reported in underlying reviews and cohorts. Measurements and outcomes: Strength, endurance, patient-reported function, complications, return-to-sport rate and timing, and post-return performance. Analysis: Narrative synthesis of underlying meta-analyses, systematic reviews, and observational cohorts; no new quantitative pooling or formal risk-of-bias appraisal was reported.
paper.findings: In a cited meta-analysis of 2,481 cases, operative treatment was associated with higher flexion strength and endurance, higher supination strength and endurance, and better MEPS and DASH scores than nonoperative treatment; these are pooled clinical associations, not randomized causal estimates. Across the reviewed athletic literature, reported return-to-sport rates after repair ranged from 91.5% to 97.5%; 65.6% returned at the same or higher intensity, while another synthesis reported 93.4% returning at any level. In an NFL cohort, 94% returned to play at a mean of 351 days; most career and performance outcomes were comparable with matched controls, although offensive linemen played fewer games per season after return. Mean return-to-sport timing across broader cohorts was approximately 6.0 to 6.3 months. Earlier return was associated with injury, surgical, and rehabilitation characteristics, but these observational associations do not establish that changing any single factor will accelerate safe return. The review advocates criteria-based rehabilitation using objective function and patient-reported outcomes rather than relying only on elapsed time.
paper.limitations: As a narrative review without reported systematic methods or formal risk-of-bias appraisal, it is vulnerable to selection and interpretation bias. The underlying studies vary in injury severity, surgical technique, sport, competitive level, rehabilitation exposure, outcome definitions, and follow-up; this is an additional transfer limitation based on the review's diverse evidence base. Operative versus nonoperative comparisons are subject to treatment-selection confounding; the reported differences should not be read as randomized causal effects. Professional-football results may inform American-football expectations but should not be directly generalized to collegiate players, other positions, or other sports. Return-to-sport percentage and time do not by themselves demonstrate restored readiness, durability, or reinjury risk.
paper.practicalImplications: For a high-demand athlete with a suspected complete rupture, the review supports prompt specialist assessment and a shared medical decision that weighs sport demands, injury features, and athlete preferences. Rehabilitation and clearance should use serial range-of-motion, strength, task-specific loading, functional testing, symptoms, and patient-reported status; a six-month average is a planning reference, not a clearance rule. Surgical technique and progression decisions remain the responsibility of the treating medical team.
